notes.3r.10: 3r.10: the sentence begins in the line before ('and it softens'); what it does not let grow is not stated. 3v.8: the 'milk' is the sap of willow bark, as the next line shows.
notes.1v.6: náttlaukr, 'night-leek', is a plant I cannot identify.
notes.2v.11: rubea (rubia) is madder; 'red-herb' renders roðagras. The earth stamped with a seal is sealed medicinal earth (terra sigillata). 'Flying serpents' (flugormar) may mean venomous creatures generally. forað, here 'substance', usually means a perilous thing or a monster; its sense here is uncertain.
notes.3v.6a: eyrsilfr is taken as quicksilver (mercury) from what is said of it; the word itself is uncertain. 'Bad noises' (óhljóð) are presumably noises in the ears.

nodes.text: and take from it both the blood and the gall, and mix both
together and put [it] in the eyes. That brightens a person's sight.
For bleeding: take the herb that grows in a wheat field, with its
leaves and red seed, and pound [it] in wine or ale,
and sing a Paternoster meanwhile, and give it him to drink.
For bleeding, if a wound bleeds: take *náttlaukr* [night-leek] and pound [it]
well, and lay it in the wound where it bleeds, and bind it on.
The herb called rubea, that is red-herb:
it drives [the child] out of a pregnant woman, even if the child is dead.
The earth on which a seal is set with a man's likeness on it:
it is good against snakebite and [the bites] of other flying serpents. And if
a man is given a poisoned drink, let him drink some of this earth;
it drives the poison out, and the man comes to no harm.
Musk is the name of a substance. It forms in the belly of an animal. It is like a kid,
[the one] that is bred in India. It runs together from
the stool in the rectum, or in another place does not let [it] grow.
If it is mixed with milk and laid on, then it is a cure.
Dioscorides says of the herb called peony:
I saw a boy eight years old who had that herb
hung around his neck. And then it happened during the day
that the herb fell off him. And at once the boy fell
down and had the falling sickness. And then it was
put back on him a second time, and then the boy came to no harm
while he had it on him. But then it fell off him a second
time, and at once he fell into the same sickness he had had
before. Then the herb was tied on him again, and he recovered
at once. And it went the same way the third time: he grew worse
when it was off, and got better when it was tied on. The same witness
Galen, the wisest of men, bears about that same herb.
Willow bark pounded with sour wine: it removes warts.
Thus said Galen: The milk that is wrung from
Mint strengthens the belly and makes the mouth sweet-smelling.
And a plaster made of mint and salt: it is good for the bite of a mad dog.
The herb called white hellebore,
mixed with milk and tempered with honey: it kills mice
if they eat of it. And its powder mixed with water and
sprinkled about the house: it kills flies.
The herb called cumin, drunk with wine: it cleanses
the bites of flying creatures. And if it is blown into a person's nostrils: it stops nosebleed.
and cleanses the bites of flying creatures. Salt and linseed, made
into a plaster: it cleanses the bites of flying creatures.
*Eyrsilfr* [quicksilver] drunk: it causes death. For into whatever
limb it runs, it scrapes [it] from inside. And if into the fire
it is put, it makes a harmful smoke. Snakes flee it,
and flying creatures die from that smoke.
